title: Markov type and superreflexivity
author: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
description: An exposition of OpenAI's proof (2026) that a real Banach space with Markov type p > 1 has an equivalent uniformly convex norm. Markov type p bounds the distance that a stationary reversible Markov chain travels in t steps by a constant times t^(1/p) times its step length. The theorem is proved from one named hypothesis, the theorem of James and Enflo that a Banach space without an equivalent uniformly convex norm has a nonreflexive space finitely representable in it. The first lesson gives the definitions, proves that Markov type bounds sums of odd edge labels of a reversible chain, and reduces the theorem to two statements. The second lesson constructs, in a space that is not superreflexive, a norm on finite sequences that is invariant under inserting zeros and does not increase under merging of neighbours. The third lesson constructs a random increasing map of a finite ordered set whose law treats all tuples alike, and a reversible chain of such maps. The fourth lesson studies four homeomorphisms of the line that play ping-pong and a sum along orbits with two levels. The fifth lesson builds the walk: n steps of norm 1 whose sum has norm at least n/24 with probability at least 3/20.
prerequisites: core course Functional Analysis (D20): normed spaces, the dual and the bidual, the Hahn-Banach theorem
finite probability: conditional means, Markov's inequality, finite Markov chains (defined in the first lesson)
Ramsey's theorem, the minimax theorem and a separation lemma, proved in the course Large independent sets in three-colorable graphs (lesson Alignment of lists: patterns, minimax and Ramsey's theorem)
the lessons prove every other fact they use, except the named hypothesis (JE) of the first lesson

checks.reading: The manuscript 'Nontrivial Markov Type Forces Superreflexivity' (OpenAI, 23 Sep 2026, in the revision of the repository on 13 Oct 2026; five sections and an appendix, two figures, 1,020 lines of TeX) was read in full on 13 Oct 2026, and every step of its argument was derived again while the lessons were written: the lattice lift for odd edge labels (detailed balance with rejected moves, the potential, the coupling up to the first rejection, the factor alpha_R); the deduction (3/20)(n/24)^p <= K^p n; the triangular arrays from Hahn-Banach and a finite form of Goldstine's theorem (including the identification of the norm of a bidual vector on the annihilator of a finite-dimensional subspace with its distance to the subspace); the spreading limit; the monotonicity under subdivision by an average over random subsets; invariance under subdivisions with varying multiplicities; same-sign merging; the convexity argument for contractive merging; the averaging lemma for charts; maximal couplings and the reversible chain of charts; the piecewise affine homeomorphisms and their four properties; the sign identity for the functions chi_s; invariance of the sum c_w under reduction; the two levels; the landmark set and the bounds 2 < y_i < 8n + 7; the transport of ranks along good steps; the partial sums of the total label; the block sums and the two lower bounds; the reduced length of a random word; the final probability 3/20. No error found. Differences of presentation, none a correction: the averaging lemma is proved with the minimax theorem of the programme in place of a separation argument in a sum norm; the spreading limit uses one application of Ramsey's theorem to k-subsets of a homogeneous set of 2k indices in place of successive thinning over the arities, and factorial indices in place of an unspecified diagonal sequence; the comparison of the procedure with the chain is not needed here; the statement that a bidual element vanishing on the annihilator of a finite-dimensional subspace lies in the subspace is proved with a dual basis. Checked by the program plan/checks_20261013/mt_check.py (seven parts, exact rational arithmetic where possible: the homeomorphisms on 560 points per letter; all 5,461 words of length at most 6 for the interior point, the invariance under reduction and the two levels; the whole walk for n = 2, 3 (all words) and n = 4 (24 words), 104 trajectories in which every step is good, with the transport of ranks, the partial sums against c_w, the block sums and the norm bound for three norms; the reduced length distribution exactly for n <= 80; the lattice lift on a small chain; the subdivision monotonicity; the elementary inequalities). All parts pass (output mt_check_run_20261013.txt). Two earlier runs did not finish for reasons in the check program: a list of test points contained duplicates, which broke a strict monotonicity test; and the first version of part 3 built a rank map over all words at once and ran out of time. Both were corrected in the program; no statement of the lessons was changed. The statement that the converse is known (Pisier; Naor, Peres, Schramm and Sheffield) and the attribution of the hypothesis to James and Enflo are taken from the manuscript; those papers were not read.

open_obligations: Named hypothesis (JE), the theorem of James and Enflo: a real Banach space that has no equivalent uniformly convex norm has a Banach space finitely representable in it that is not reflexive. It is not proved in the programme (it combines James's characterization of reflexivity with Enflo's renorming theorem). The main theorem depends on it; the walk with linear displacement (fifth lesson) and all lemmas of lessons 3 and 4 do not.
The Hahn-Banach theorem and the isometric embedding of a normed space into its bidual are taken from the core course Functional Analysis (D20); the exact locator in its text has not been looked up.
Not in the course: the converse (a superreflexive space has Markov type p for some p > 1), which the first lesson quotes from the manuscript; complex Banach spaces.
The history of the question (Ball; Naor's question) is not told in the lessons and was not checked.
The lessons were written and checked by one model in one session; they have not been checked by a second reader.
